questions.q: How many broad traits does the Big Five describe, and what are they called here?
questions.do: Read the introduction and the results headings.
questions.a: Five: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability and Intellect/Imagination.

questions.q: Why do some statements count in reverse?
questions.do: Compare statement 1 (“Am the life of the party”) with statement 6 (“Don’t talk a lot”).
questions.a: They describe the opposite end of a trait, so agreeing with them lowers that trait’s score. Mixing both directions stops people from just agreeing with everything.

questions.q: What is the lowest and highest possible score for one trait?
questions.do: Read the note above your results.
questions.a: From 10 to 50: ten statements, each scored 1 to 5.

questions.q: How is this different from a horoscope?
questions.a: The result comes only from your own answers, and the same answers always give the same result. A horoscope depends only on a date.

questions.q: Where do these fifty statements come from, and who may use them?
questions.a: The International Personality Item Pool, from psychologist Lewis Goldberg’s Big-Five markers. It is in the public domain, free for anyone.
